[Lab 7: Collaborative Bio Data Science using git and GitHub via RStudio](https://r4bds.github.io/lab07.html)

## Background

This is a micro-report based on a blog post: [“PCA tidyverse style”](https://clauswilke.com/blog/2020/09/07/pca-tidyverse-style/) by Claus O. Wilke, Professor of Integrative Biology.

> *Doing a PCA in R is easy: Just run the function `prcomp()` on your matrix of scaled numeric predictor variables. There’s just one problem, however. The result is an object of class `prcomp` that doesn’t fit nicely into the tidyverse framework, e.g. for visualization. While it’s reasonably easy to extract the relevant info with [some base-R manipulations,](https://wilkelab.org/classes/SDS348/2020_spring/worksheets/class9_solutions.html) I’ve never been happy with this approach. But now, I’ve realized that all the necessary functions to do this tidyverse-style are available in the broom package.*
>
> \- Claus O. Wilke

## Aim

The goal of this assignment is to use "tidyverse" and "broom" packages to perform PCA in RStudio.

### Load libraries

To fulfill this objective, the following libraries are loaded in the working environment.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)  # devtools::install_github("tidymodels/broom")
library(cowplot) # for plot themes
```

### Load data

We will analyze the `biopsy` dataset from the MASS package, which contains breast tumor biopsy data collected by Dr. William H. Wolberg at the University of Wisconsin Hospitals in Madison. Breast tumor biopsies from a total of 699 patients were analyzed. The dataset contains nine attributes, each scored on a scale of 1 to 10. Each tumor’s diagnosis (benign/malignant) is also recorded.

The raw data is publicly available and is fetched into the working environment.

```{r}
biopsy <- read_csv("https://wilkelab.org/classes/SDS348/data_sets/biopsy.csv")
```

## PCA

> *In general, when performing PCA, we’ll want to do (at least) three things:*
>
> 1.  *Look at the data in PC coordinates.*
>
> 2.  *Look at the rotation matrix.*
>
> 3.  *Look at the variance explained by each PC.*
>
> \- Claus O. Wilke

### Looking at the data in PC coordinates

We start by running the PCA and storing the result in a variable `pca_fit`. There are two issues to consider here:

-   First, the `prcomp()` function can only deal with numeric columns, so we need to remove all non-numeric columns from the data. This is straightforward using the `where(is.numeric)` tidyselect construct.

-   Second, we normally want to scale the data values to unit variance before PCA. We do so by using the argument `scale = TRUE` in `prcomp()`.

```{r}
pca_fit <- biopsy |>  
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>  # retain only numeric columns
  prcomp(scale = TRUE)          # do PCA on scaled data
```

As an alternative to `scale = TRUE`, we could also have scaled the data by explicitly invoking the `scale()` function.

```{r}
pca_fit <- biopsy |>  
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>    # retain only numeric columns
  scale() |>                      # scale data
  prcomp()                        # do PCA
```

Now, we want to plot the data in PC coordinates. In general, this means combining the PC coordinates with the original dataset, so we can color points according to categorical variables present in the original data that were removed for the PCA. In our case, the pathological outcome of the biopsied tumors. We do this with the `augment()` function from broom, which takes as arguments the fitted model and the original data. The columns containing the fitted coordinates are called `.fittedPC1`, `.fittedPC2`, etc.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1
#| fig-cap: "PC1-PC2 plot"
pca_fit |> 
  augment(biopsy) |>              # add original dataset back in
  ggplot(aes(.fittedPC1, 
             .fittedPC2, 
             color = outcome)) +# add the color code to discriminate outcome
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(malignant = "#FF87BF", 
                                benign = "#71D2F5")) +
  theme_half_open(12) +         # clean appreance without contour grids 
  background_grid() +
  labs(title = "Fig.1: Benign and malignant samples scattered \n according to PC1 and PC2")
```

### Looking at the rotation matrix

Next, we plot the rotation matrix. The rotation matrix is stored as `pca_fit$rotation`, but here we’ll extract it using the `tidy()` function from broom. When applied to `prcomp` objects, the `tidy()` function takes an additional argument `matrix`, which we set to `matrix = "rotation"` to extract the rotation matrix.

```{r}
# extract rotation matrix
pca_fit |>
  tidy(matrix = "rotation")
```

Now in the context of a plot:

```{r}
# define arrow style for plotting
arrow_style <- arrow(
  angle = 20, ends = "first", type = "closed", length = grid::unit(8, "pt")
)

# plot rotation matrix and re-arrange columns according to PC n°
pca_fit |>
  tidy(matrix = "rotation") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = "PC",        # adds columns corresponding to each PC
              names_prefix = "PC", 
              values_from = "value") |> # rewrites rotation values in each column
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_segment(xend = 0, 
               yend = 0, 
               arrow = arrow_style) +
  geom_text(aes(label = column),
                hjust = 1, 
                nudge_x = -0.02, 
                color = "#D1387A") +
  xlim(-1.25, .5) + 
  ylim(-.5, 1) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_linedraw() +
  labs(
    title = "Fig.2: PCA - Rotation Matrix plot") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5))
  

```

### Look at the variance explained by each PC

Finally, we’ll plot the variance explained by each PC. We can again extract this information using the `tidy()` function from broom, now by setting the `matrix` argument to `matrix = "eigenvalues"`.

```{r}
pca_fit %>%
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues")
```

Now in the context of a plot.

```{r}

# Create a bar plot binned by PC
pca_fit %>%
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues") %>%
  ggplot(aes(PC, percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +          # defining the labels for each PC 1-9
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01))
  ) +
  theme_minimal_hgrid(12)                    # lighter grid for cleaner visuals


# Same but with a title
pca_fit |> 
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, 
             y = percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#ED9FCC", 
           alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Fig3: % Variance explained by each PC") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01))) +
  theme_minimal_hgrid(12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

The first component captures 65% of the variation in the data and, as we can see from the first plot in this post, nicely separates the benign samples from the malignant samples. According to the eigenvalues data, 74% of the variance in the dataset is explained by the first to principal components, which is qualitatively illustrated with @fig-1.
